What the Decision Index is

The Decision Index is one number per model for how well an open reproduction of TypeSafe's Jev makes typed decisions: pick an option, a label, a tool, a ranking, a probability. Every entrant faces the same frozen suite of 120,340 requests across 36 static benchmarks, a fixed subset of the request set Jev jev-1.13.0 was scored on, with Jev's answers recorded once and never re-run.

The index averages 38 benchmarks in 5 weighted capability areas. Each benchmark keeps its own primary metric, and a request the model could not answer counts as wrong, so the number rewards breadth and honesty over cherry-picking. Every benchmark is chance-corrected before averaging, so 0 means random guessing and 100 means perfect. It is a point estimate on a fixed panel; nothing is tuned to the entrants. Decision Index 0.2.1 keeps the 0.2 benchmarks and rules with these changes: RouterBench and SGD leave the index (38 benchmarks remain); areas are sized by √n with Arts & Human Taste fixed at 10%, and gold ★ benchmarks weigh 1.2 inside their area; ACOS, ToolRet, BRIGHT, RAGTruth and Home appliances are rescored as described under Rescored benchmarks.

Formally: sum_b(0.2*benchmark[b]) per area, 100*(0.2585*category[knowledge] + 0.2585*category[language] + 0.2002*category[retrieval] + 0.1828*category[tools] + 0.1000*category[arts]) for the index, on the panel decision-index-0.2.1. The index is the chance-corrected score; raw accuracy is shown alongside it and the breadth variant is computed and hidden (below).

Three kinds of benchmark

Original-task benchmarks: published questions, answer spaces and scoring retained; extraction of a clearly labeled supported subset or random sampling does not by itself create a new task.
Jev-adapted benchmarks: published source data or environment, with a decision interface, answer construction, candidate retrieval, partner protocol or evaluated objective adapted for Jev.
Purpose-built benchmarks: new local scenarios and evaluation logic; currently the executable home-appliance benchmark.

Metrics exclude failed/incomplete cases; coverage is explicit. No silent replacement of failures. Different primary metrics are not averaged across benchmarks. Latency includes HTTPS and concurrent service scheduling; not isolated model inference. Full raw HTTP responses/payloads and all retry timings are in http-attempts.jsonl. BPoMP/RouterBench/GSM8K and chunked tasks retain all linked requests for sampled cases. Original 500-case pilot remains frozen separately. Request caps count planned logical evaluations. Transport retries or context splits are logged separately and may add HTTP attempts. Cached successful pilot responses reused only for identical full request SHA256; original latency and provenance retained. Game protocols and budgets are pinned separately. Release v2 keeps every v1 row except a stratified subset cut of ToolRet (1,000 of 7,961 queries incl. excluded ones) and BRIGHT (550 of 1,384 queries); all other benchmarks, question order, options and scoring are unchanged. Kept ToolRet and BRIGHT queries retain their complete candidate lists. ToolRet and BRIGHT rows of questions listed in excluded-questions.json were carried over unchanged (they are never scored); the scored subsets are 1,000 and 550 query groups, see scored_cases.

The 442 excluded questions

Questions dropped from scoring for every engine so no model is graded on a case another model was structurally unable to attempt.

A row is excluded for reach only when nearly the whole field cannot attempt it. A limit that one model has and others do not is that model's result, not a defect in the suite, and is never grounds for removing the row. unchanged; selected-rows.jsonl.gz and its sha256 are untouched. Exclusion is applied at scoring time only. Defects verified against the upstream sources; cais/mmlu ships the duplicate choices verbatim and the builder applies no normalisation to MMLU.

Adaptation classes: A_direct — Original finite choices, class labels, or probabilities map directly; only parsing, serialization and label mapping are needed. B_mechanical — Extra deterministic processing changes the evaluated view: filtering, extraction, search, enumeration, pairing, simulation or numeric encoding. No per-item semantic option authoring. C_semantic_options — The adaptation relies on authored semantic option spaces/scenarios or model-generated candidate answers absent from the original native answer format. not_applicable — Removed, skipped, or unspecified; no active adaptation classification. Licences are read from the archived source repository or dataset card and describe that artefact, not necessarily every text inside it; public availability is not a blanket grant to republish the underlying benchmark content.

Index formula

Exactly as implemented in build_leaderboard.py over compute_indices.py.

BENCHMARK SCOREsb = primary metric of b over all scoreable cases · a case with any failed or unsupported request scores 0
CHANCE-CORRECTEDkb = clip((sb − rb) / (1 − rb)) · rb is what random guessing scores on b (table below)
AREA SCOREKc = Σb ∈ Bc gb · kb / Σ gb · g = 1.2 for gold ★, 1.0 otherwise
DECISION INDEXI = 100 · Σc wc · Kc · five areas, wc ∝ √nc for the four core areas, Arts fixed at 0.1: Knowledge 25.8%, Language 25.8%, Retrieval 20.0%, Tools 18.3%, Arts 10.0%, 38 benchmarks · 0 = random guessing, 100 = perfect
RAW ACCURACYIraw = 100 · Σc wc · (1 / |Bc|) · Σb sb · not chance-corrected, shown on model pages
LOWER IS BETTERsForecastBench = clip((0.25 − Brier) / (0.25 − 0)) · coverage · 0 at the baseline (always predict p = 0.5) or worse
HIDDEN · BREADTHIbreadth = 100 · ( Πc (0.1 + 0.9 · Kc)wc − 0.1 ) / 0.9
Score every benchmark with its own primary metric and adjust it for coverage: an unanswered, refused, errored or unsupported request counts as wrong (for the 19 core25 static benchmarks a case whose linked requests did not all succeed scores zero; for the others the score on answered requests is multiplied by the answered share).
Benchmarks with several tracks (RouterBench 0-shot/5-shot, GSM8K 4-/10-choice) average their tracks equally; iSarcasmEval uses track A English as its headline and track B never enters the index.

Chance correction

The Decision Index is chance-corrected. Every benchmark score is first mapped to (score − chance) / (1 − chance), clipped to 0–1, where chance is what random guessing scores on that benchmark: 0.5 on a yes/no question, 0.25 with four options, the expected nDCG of a random ranking for retrieval, the F1 of random labels for F1-scored tasks. 0 means no better than random guessing and 100 means perfect, so a benchmark made of yes/no questions no longer hands out 50 free points and a benchmark with hundreds of options no longer looks harder than it is. Area scores and the index average these corrected values exactly as before. The raw, uncorrected accuracy is still computed and shown on each model page as raw accuracy (not chance-corrected).

Rules of the game

Every entrant runs as published, on the whole suite, and is scored against the full denominator.

No truncation

Every request is sent whole. A model whose context window cannot hold a prompt records that request as unsupported; it is never shortened to fit.

No label filtering

The full option set of every question is offered. No option pruning, no candidate reduction, no label-set narrowing per model.

No prompt tuning

Each entrant runs with its own native inference helpers, prompts and readout rules as published. Mechanical schema translations and any probability conversion are recorded with the adapter.

No labels in the adapter

Gold answers never enter model state; requests.jsonl carries the exact payloads with labels omitted.

No correctness-based retry

Transient transport errors retry up to twice; a valid wrong answer is never retried.

Native abstentions stand

A model that abstains keeps its abstention as a terminal answer; the wrapper never forces it into a listed option.

Unanswered = wrong

Unsupported, refused and errored requests score zero against the full denominator. Nobody climbs by skipping the hard cases.

Complete-run gate

A run enters the index only when its status event is "complete" and it has processed at least 119,898 rows (the 120,340-request corpus minus the 442 questions excluded for every engine).

Latency

Two different clocks: in-process GPU time for the reproductions, an HTTP round trip for Jev.

Reproductions · on the GPU

Latency is measured on its own, after scoring: every entrant runs the same 750 rows (stratified by benchmark and prompt length across the 0.2 scope, plus 10 untimed warm-up rows) as one process sending one request at a time on 1 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000, using the fastest inference path the model or its code supports. The figure is the wall time of one row, request in to all answers out, measured the same way for in-process and HTTP engines; board medians and p95s come from this run, not from the scoring runs.

Median and p95 over the timed rows that returned an answer; per-benchmark medians are shown only where the sample holds at least 5 rows of that benchmark. A bootstrap on the full single-process runs of ten entrants put the sample median within 5% and the p95 within 10% of a full run at 95% confidence. Earlier board figures came from the scoring runs, some timed with 6 to 12 processes sharing a card or with queue waits removed; they are no longer shown.

Jev · hosted HTTP
HTTP median 253 ms · p95 437 ms · total median 950 ms · 132,422 requests

Jev is TypeSafe's hosted API: a network round-trip from our lab with one sequential HTTPS client on the same latency sample, not comparable to on-card latency. Its answers on this sample drifted from the Sep-19 board rows (20 choice flips); Jev's scores are unchanged.

Remote hosted API measured over HTTP. total_wall_ms includes client retries and network; http_wall_ms is the request itself. Local GPU reproductions have no network leg, so these are not a controlled speed comparison.

The leaderboard plots the reproductions' single-process time against Jev's HTTPS round trip on one axis for orientation only. The two are not a controlled speed comparison: Jev's number includes the network and shared service scheduling, the reproductions' numbers include none of that.

Changelog
Edition v0.2.1 · 2026-09-28
New area weights: Arts & Human Taste is fixed at 10%; the other four areas share the rest in proportion to the square root of their benchmark count: Tools & Automation 18.3%, Retrieval & Classification 20.0%, Knowledge & Reasoning 25.8%, Language Understanding 25.8%.
Gold ★ benchmarks weigh 1.2 inside their area, the rest 1.0: MMLU-Pro, BBH, GPQA Diamond, HLE, ANLI, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, BANKING77, CLINC150, BRIGHT, BFCL, API-Bank, ForecastBench.
SGD leaves the index until it is re-run with a fixed builder, and RouterBench leaves because its prompt gives away the best route. Both stay on the board.
ACOS is now scored with F1 per review instead of all-or-nothing, and stays in the index.
ToolRet and BRIGHT count only queries with at least one relevant candidate among the 32 (685 of 1,000 and 220 of 550); chance is recomputed on the same queries.
RAGTruth chance is now always answering "hallucinated" (F1 0.518) instead of a fair coin (0.411).
Home appliances drops 24 duplicate test rows and 48 rows identical to published dev rows (88 of 160 kept).
Surogate Rune 26B-A4B v3 replaces v1 on the board: the author's submitted run, adopted after our 3,000-row reproduction matched it exactly.
reflex 27B's full-coverage rerun replaces its 26-option run on the board: the author's submitted run with wide-choice labels, adopted after our single-card latency run agreed with it within reflex's own run-to-run noise.
Hopper (G) 1.2 replaces Hopper 1.1.1 on the board: the author's submitted run of the next Hopper adapter (same base and serving code), adopted after our single-card latency run agreed with it within the A10G-vs-RTX noise.
Edition v0.2 · 2026-09-27
Scores are now chance-corrected: 0 means random guessing and 100 means perfect, so yes/no questions no longer give free points.
30 new models on the board, plus newer versions of 14 existing ones.
The index now counts 40 benchmarks, up from 19: 7 brand-new ones (MMLU-Pro, BBH, When2Call, RAGTruth, HoVer, New Yorker caption matching, PhishNChips), plus 15 we already ran that now count, such as HLE, ANLI, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, BANKING77 and CLINC150.
MMLU left the index: top models have nearly maxed it out, and MMLU-Pro takes its place. ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge are still shown but don't count.
ToolRet and BRIGHT are run on a subset of their data that doesn't skew results but is faster and cheaper to run.
Edition v0.1 · 2026-09-22
First public edition: 31 open reproductions plus Jev jev-1.13.0 on the frozen 132,422-request suite.
442 defective or out-of-reach questions excluded for every engine alike; 131,980 scoreable rows.
Panel: core25 with the six interactive environments left out (19 static benchmarks, five equal-weight areas); ChessBench folded into Knowledge & Reasoning; Language & Retrieval split into Language Understanding and Retrieval & Classification.

Other
Contrastive rankers such as CLM-v0.1-8B do poorly when the option texts are bare labels (yes/no, NotMentioned): scored by similarity, the label carries almost nothing to rank, and CLM picks NotMentioned on all of ContractNLI, yes on 99% of BFCL decisions and no on all of ForecastBench (artifacts/jev-reproductions/investigations/clm-v0.1-8b-investigation/).
Xor runs on a single RTX PRO 6000 with tensor parallelism 1, as every entrant runs on one card for fairness; the author validated the model at tensor parallelism 2 on two cards, and only the tensor-parallel split and the static memory fraction differ from that configuration.
Reproduce it

The runner, scorers, index computation and this page's data build live in the open at github.com/apolinario/decision-index. Run an entrant on the frozen corpus with run.py, score it with report_model.py, mine its refusals with answer_gaps.py, recompute the panel with compute_indices.py, and rebuild data/index.json and data/methodology.json with build_leaderboard.py and build_methodology.py. The corpus, chance baselines, panel proposal and exclusion manifest are pinned by sha256 in the JSON above, so a re-run that changes any of them announces itself.
